Format is not the issue. Only 13–16% of wrong finished answers contain the gold number anywhere, and only 6–8% near the end, so the model mostly never computes the right answer. Algebra-style answers end in the Minerva/MATH convention, "Final Answer: The final answer is $\boxed{43}$", which the grader reads correctly since that is the last number. There is no sign of deliberate final-step sabotage.

The one exception is cut markdown answers: 37% of them (16 of 43) contain the gold number somewhere, but the model kept going until the token limit, and the "last number" became something else. I want to see what happens after the gold appears in those cases. If the model reaches the right answer and then runs on (re-verifying, restating, looping on other numbers), a stopping failure accounts for a few points. If the gold appears only by coincidence in an intermediate step, there is nothing to gain there.

I will print, for a few such cases, the text around the first occurrence of the gold and the start of the loop.

The gold numbers in those cut answers are coincidences: a step label ("4."), or an intermediate value later misused (21 − 14 = 7, then 7 − 14 = −7). So there is no near-miss or stopping mechanism. The failures are genuine reasoning errors in both styles.

One classic hiding signature remains untested: late layers overriding a correct choice that intermediate layers already favour. That is the "overthinking" pattern (Halawi et al.), which a sandbagging fine-tune would plausibly create, because fine-tuning often changes late layers most.

I will run a teacher-forced pass on 150 DEV reference solutions, returning residual states for layers 12–26 and the final top-20 tokens. In the kernel I then compute a logit lens restricted to plausible tokens: each layer's residual (with the final-norm scale) projected onto the unembedding rows of the final top-20 plus the reference token. I track the reference token's log-prob across layers at decision tokens (first digits of chosen quantities, words) and at copy tokens, as a control.

If decision tokens peak at an intermediate layer and lose probability in the last layers while copy tokens do not, a late-layer brake is localized. A monotonic rise to the final layer closes the line.

The text file is ready. I now run the logit-lens pass on the original model: 150 reference solutions, residual states after layers 12–26, the final top-20 candidates and token log-probs. Layer 26 is the last residual before the final norm, so its restricted log-probs double as a check that my projection matches the model's real outputs.
